subject: bio
title: B1 – Protein Synthesis
outcomesHtml:
The candidate is able at least in health and food production contexts to explain how self-regulation takes place at molecular level, using the concepts of DNA and protein synthesis.

Specimen contexts:

  • Health and healthcare: Human geneticists at university hospitals are doing experimental DNA research to enable Duchenne muscular dystrophy patients to produce functional dystrophin.
  • Food production: Biotechnologists at the Bureau for Genetically Modified Organisms (Bureau GGO) are assessing applications for the use of genetically modified crops in order to ensure that they are safe for humans and the environment.
  • Food production: Food technologists at a food production company are changing DNA and thus protein synthesis in order to produce healthier products (functional foods).

B1.1 — DNA

Specification:

The candidate is able in a particular context to:

  1. describe the structure of DNA and RNA and explain the differences
  2. list the functions of DNA, mRNA, tRNA and rRNA and describe how they relate to their structure
  3. explain how the base sequence in DNA can be identified.

Specific concepts:

Nucleic acids, helical structure, base pairing, nucleotide, single-strand and double-strand DNA, chromosomes, nucleosomes, histones, nucleic DNA, mitochondrial and chloroplast mtDNA, cDNA, RNA, genetic code, plasmid, primer, PCR, sequences, restriction enzyme, repetitive DNA.

B1.2 — Protein Synthesis

Specification:

The candidate is able in a particular context to:

  1. explain how proteins are produced, based on the relationship between triplet code and amino acid
  2. describe the process of transcription and translation
  3. explain how the amino acid sequence (primary structure) of a protein determines its structure and mechanism
  4. explain how proteins determine the structure and mechanism of biological units.

Specific concepts:

Amino acid, primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure, protein, peptide binding, transcription, translation, mRNA, tRNA, rRNA, cytoplasm, ribosome, Golgi apparatus, rough endoplasmic reticulum, triplet code, codon, anticodon, coding strand, reading direction, template/matrix strand, DNA polymerase, start codon, stop codon, plasmid.
notesHtml:
B1 — Protein Synthesis: notes

These are English explanations of every learning outcome in README.md. Status: reviewed against the CCVX syllabus (21 September 2017) and standard VWO biology; not yet checked against an open source text or exam question. Diagrams are original SVGs.

  • In Dutch VWO: central exam (CE).
  • Dutch source: CvTE syllabus biologie vwo 2027 (version 2, July 2025), M1 Eiwitsynthese (M1.1–M1.2). A citation like (CvTE M1.2 spec 2) means specification 2 of M1.2; its numbers don't match the CCVX numbers.

Dutch terms are in brackets. Binas tables are named, not numbered, because the numbers differ between editions.

B1.1 DNA

1. Structure of DNA and RNA

  • DNA and RNA are nucleic acids (nucleïnezuren): long chains of nucleotides. (CvTE M1.1 specs 1–2)
  • A nucleotide has three parts: a phosphate group, a sugar with five carbon atoms and a nitrogenous base.
  • DNA has the sugar deoxyribose and the bases adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C); RNA has the sugar ribose and uracil (U) instead of thymine. The chemistry is in chemistry G01.
  • The phosphate of one nucleotide is bonded to the sugar of the next, so each strand has a sugar–phosphate backbone with the bases sticking out to one side.
  • The carbon atoms of the sugar are numbered 1' to 5'. A strand starts at a 5' end (free phosphate on carbon 5') and stops at a 3' end (free –OH on carbon 3'), so it has a direction.
  • Single-strand and double-strand DNA (enkelstrengs DNA, dubbelstrengs DNA): DNA is normally a double strand, two antiparallel strands (one runs 5'→3', the other 3'→5') held together by hydrogen bonds (waterstofbruggen) between their bases (chemistry B03).
  • Single-stranded DNA exists only briefly, when the strands are pulled apart to be copied or read (and in PCR), and permanently in a few viruses such as bacteriophage φX174.
  • Base pairing (basenparing) is complementary: A pairs with T through two hydrogen bonds and G with C through three. A double-ring base (A, G) always faces a single-ring base (T, C), so the double strand is equally wide everywhere.
  • One strand therefore fixes the other: 5'-ATGC-3' pairs with 3'-TACG-5'.

Part of a DNA double strand (original diagram). The two sugar–phosphate backbones are antiparallel (5'→3' opposite 3'→5'). Base pairing is complementary: A–T with two hydrogen bonds (dashed), G–C with three. That is why %A = %T and %G = %C in double-stranded DNA.

  • In double-stranded DNA %A = %T and %G = %C: DNA with 30% A has 30% T, 20% G and 20% C.
  • DNA rich in G–C pairs needs more heat to separate its strands: 10 base pairs with 4 G–C and 6 A–T pairs are held by 4 × 3 + 6 × 2 = 24 hydrogen bonds.
  • The two strands wind around each other into a double helix (helical structure, helixstructuur) about 2 nm wide, with one full turn about every 10 base pairs (3.4 nm).
  • RNA is a single strand and much shorter; it can fold back on itself where its own bases pair, as in the cloverleaf shape of tRNA (outcome 2).
DNA RNA
Sugar deoxyribose ribose
Bases A, T, G, C A, U, G, C
Strands two, as a double helix one, often folded
Length very long (millions of base pairs) short (one gene or less)
Where nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts made in the nucleus, works mainly outside it
  • In eukaryotes each chromosome (chromosoom) is one very long DNA molecule packed with proteins (eiwitten); a human body cell has 46 chromosomes in its nucleus.
  • The DNA is wound around histones (histonen): small, positively charged proteins that attract the negatively charged phosphate groups.
  • A nucleosome (nucleosoom) is a core of eight histone proteins with about 150 base pairs of DNA wrapped almost twice around it; with linker DNA in between, nucleosomes look like beads on a string. (CvTE M4.1 spec 4)
  • The string of nucleosomes coils and folds further, and before a cell divides it condenses into compact chromosomes that are visible under a light microscope (E02).
  • Tightly packed DNA can't be read, so packing also helps switch genes (genen) off (D01).
  • Bacteria have one circular chromosome without histones, lying free in the cell, and often extra small DNA circles called plasmids (plasmiden, outcome 3).
  • Trap: %A = %T and %G = %C only hold for double-stranded DNA; they don't apply to a single strand, to mRNA or to a single-stranded virus.

2. Functions of DNA, mRNA, tRNA and rRNA

  • DNA stores the hereditary information in its base sequence (basenvolgorde); a gene is a stretch of DNA whose sequence codes for one RNA, usually an mRNA that codes for a protein. (CvTE M1.1 specs 3–4)
  • DNA's structure suits storage and copying: each of the two complementary strands carries the full information, so either strand can serve as the template for replication (DNA-replicatie, E01) or repair.
  • DNA is also chemically more stable than RNA, because deoxyribose lacks the extra –OH group that makes RNA easy to break down.
  • mRNA (messenger RNA) is a single-stranded copy of one gene that carries the code from the nucleus to the ribosomes (ribosomen) as a row of codons.
  • mRNA is broken down within minutes to hours, so a cell can stop making a protein quickly by stopping transcription (transcriptie, B1.2 outcome 2).
  • tRNA (transfer RNA) is a short RNA of about 75–90 nucleotides that folds into a cloverleaf by base pairing within its own strand; one loop carries the anticodon and the 3' end carries the matching amino acid (aminozuur).
  • A specific enzyme loads each tRNA with its own amino acid, which makes tRNA the adapter between a codon and an amino acid.
  • rRNA (ribosomal RNA) forms the two subunits of a ribosome together with proteins; it binds the mRNA and the tRNAs and itself catalyses the peptide bond (peptidebinding) between the amino acids.
  • Bacterial ribosomes are smaller and built differently from those in our cells, so antibiotics such as streptomycin and tetracycline block bacterial translation (translatie) and leave ours alone (B05).
  • Nuclear DNA (CCVX: “nucleic DNA”, kern-DNA) lies in the linear chromosomes of the nucleus, packed with histones; it holds almost all genes and comes from both parents.
  • CCVX's “mitochondrial and chloroplast mtDNA” means mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA, mitochondriaal DNA) and chloroplast DNA (cpDNA, chloroplast DNA): small circular molecules without histones, like bacterial DNA, which supports the endosymbiotic theory (F04).
  • Human mtDNA has about 16,600 base pairs and 37 genes (13 for proteins of cellular respiration, 22 for tRNAs, 2 for rRNAs); it passes on only through the egg cell, so it comes from the mother (E03).
  • Chloroplast DNA codes for some photosynthesis proteins, such as the large subunit of the enzyme rubisco, and for the chloroplast's own rRNA and tRNA; most proteins of both organelles are coded by nuclear genes.
  • Repetitive DNA (repetitief DNA) makes up about half of the human genome (genoom): sequences that occur many times and mostly don't code for protein.
  • Tandem repeats lie head to tail: telomeres are the sequence TTAGGG repeated many times at the chromosome ends (E02), and short tandem repeats (STRs) are units of 2–6 bases repeated a variable number of times.
  • Other repeats are copies of transposons (jumping genes) scattered over all chromosomes.
  • The number of repeats in an STR differs between people, which makes STRs the basis of DNA profiling (E01).
  • Trap: tRNA and rRNA are never translated: their genes are only transcribed, and the folded RNA is the working product. Only mRNA is translated into protein.

3. Identifying the base sequence

  • To read the base sequence of a piece of DNA it is sequenced, but first the piece is cut out with restriction enzymes (restrictie-enzymen) and multiplied by PCR or in bacteria with plasmids. CCVX's “sequences” corresponds to the CvTE's sequencen: sequencing, reading the order of the bases. (CvTE M1.1 spec 5)
  • A restriction enzyme cuts double-stranded DNA at a specific recognition sequence of usually 4–8 base pairs, often a palindrome that reads the same on both strands from 5' to 3'.
  • Example: EcoRI cuts GAATTC between G and A on both strands, leaving single-stranded sticky ends AATT that can pair with any other end cut by EcoRI.
  • In random DNA a given 6-base site occurs on average once every 4⁶ = 4096 base pairs; enzymes with a 4-base site (once every 4⁴ = 256) cut much more often.
  • Bacteria use restriction enzymes to cut up the DNA of invading bacteriophages, and they protect their own DNA by methylating its recognition sites.
  • Gel electrophoresis (gelelektroforese): the phosphate groups make DNA fragments negatively charged, so in an electric field they move through a gel towards the positive pole, short fragments faster than long ones. The gel sorts fragments by length.
  • PCR (polymerase chain reaction, polymerasekettingreactie) copies one chosen stretch of DNA in a tube by repeating a cycle of three temperature steps:
    • denaturation (denaturatie) at about 95 °C: the hydrogen bonds break and the strands separate;
    • annealing at about 50–65 °C: the primers bind to their complementary sites on either side of the target;
    • extension at about 72 °C: a heat-stable DNA polymerase (DNA-polymerase), the enzyme that builds DNA, adds free nucleotides to the 3' end of each primer; it comes from the hot-spring bacterium Thermus aquaticus (Taq polymerase).
  • Each cycle doubles the number of copies, so one double strand gives 2ⁿ after n cycles: 2³⁰ ≈ 1.07·10⁹ after 30 cycles, in theory, at 100% efficiency.
  • Strictly, double strands of exactly the target length (primer to primer) first appear in cycle 3; after n cycles there are 2ⁿ − 2n of them, so after 30 cycles practically every copy is the target fragment.
  • A primer is a short single strand of DNA, for PCR about 20 synthetic nucleotides, complementary to the 3' end of the target on one strand. DNA polymerase can only extend an existing 3' end, so copying starts at the primers.
  • Twenty bases are enough to be unique: a given 20-base sequence is expected by chance only once in 4²⁰ ≈ 1.1·10¹² bases, more than 300 times the human genome of about 3.2·10⁹ base pairs.
  • A plasmid is a small circular DNA molecule in bacteria (and yeast), separate from the chromosome, that is copied on its own and often carries genes for antibiotic resistance.
  • To clone a fragment, the plasmid and the fragment are cut with the same restriction enzyme, their sticky ends pair, DNA ligase seals them, and bacteria that take up the recombinant plasmid copy it every time they divide (E01, D01).
  • Sanger sequencing: DNA polymerase copies the fragment from a primer in a mix with a few chain-stopping nucleotides (dideoxynucleotides), each base with its own fluorescent colour. This gives fragments that end at every position; sorted by length, their colours give the sequence base by base.
  • Modern machines sequence millions of fragments at once, which made reading whole genomes fast and cheap; the Human Genome Project finished its sequence in 2003.
  • cDNA (complementary DNA) is DNA copied from mature mRNA by the enzyme reverse transcriptase, which comes from retroviruses such as HIV. (CvTE M3.1 spec 2)
  • cDNA has no introns (C01), so it shows a gene's coding sequence directly and can be expressed in bacteria, which can't remove introns.
  • Once a sequence is known, the Binas table of the genetic code (genetische code) gives the amino acids it codes for, and comparing sequences reveals mutations (mutaties) and kinship (F01).
  • Trap: PCR doesn't copy the whole DNA, only the stretch between the two primers; you have to know the sequences on both sides of the target to design them.

B1.2 Protein Synthesis

1. Triplet code and amino acids

  • A protein (eiwit, proteïne) is a chain of amino acids; cells use 20 different amino acids, and their order is coded in the base sequence of a gene. (CvTE M1.2 spec 1)
  • The code is a triplet code (tripletcode): three bases code for one amino acid. A doublet code would give only 4² = 16 combinations, too few for 20 amino acids, while triplets give 4³ = 64.
  • A codon is a triplet in the mRNA; the Binas table of the genetic code gives the amino acid for each of the 64 mRNA codons.
  • 61 codons code for amino acids; the 3 stop codons (stopcodons) UAA, UAG and UGA end translation, because no tRNA fits them.
  • The start codon (startcodon) AUG codes for methionine and marks where translation starts, so every new chain begins with methionine (often removed later).
  • The code is degenerate: most amino acids have several codons (leucine, serine and arginine six each; methionine and tryptophan only one), so a change in the third base often doesn't change the amino acid.
  • Codons don't overlap and have no gaps between them, so the start codon fixes the reading frame for the rest of the mRNA.
  • The code is nearly universal: bacteria, plants and animals read codons the same way, so a human gene works in a bacterium. There are small exceptions, for example in mitochondria (F01).
  • Deleting one nucleotide shifts the reading frame (leesraamverschuiving): AUG CCA GAU GGC UGG UAA (Met–Pro–Asp–Gly–Trp–stop) becomes AUG CAG AUG GCU GGU AA… (Met–Gln–Met–Ala–Gly…), while deleting three nucleotides removes just one amino acid.
  • Trap: you can derive the amino acid sequence from a DNA sequence, but not one unique DNA sequence from an amino acid sequence, because most amino acids have several codons.

2. Transcription and translation

  • In transcription (transcriptie) a gene is copied into mRNA in the nucleus; in translation (translatie) ribosomes in the cytoplasm (cytoplasma), the cell contents outside the nucleus, use the mRNA to link amino acids into a chain. (CvTE M1.2 spec 2)
  • RNA polymerase (RNA-polymerase) binds to the promoter (promotor), a DNA sequence in front of the gene, opens the double strand and starts building RNA without a primer. (CvTE M3.1 spec 3)
  • The template strand (CCVX: “template/matrix strand”, template/matrijsstreng) is the strand that is read: RNA polymerase pairs free RNA nucleotides with it (A–U, T–A, G–C, C–G).
  • The coding strand (coderende streng) is the other strand: it has the same sequence as the mRNA, with T instead of U, so you can read the codons straight from it.
  • Reading direction (afleesrichting): nucleic acids are always built 5'→3', so the template is read 3'→5'. The ribosome reads the mRNA 5'→3' from start codon to stop codon, and the protein grows from its amino end to its carboxyl end.
  • Exam questions give either strand: from a template strand, write the complementary bases with U opposite A; from a coding strand, just replace T by U.
  • Worked example: template strand 3'-TAC GGT CTA ATT-5', coding strand 5'-ATG CCA GAT TAA-3' → mRNA 5'-AUG CCA GAU UAA-3' → Met–Pro–Asp–stop.
  • At the end of the gene RNA polymerase lets go. In eukaryotes the pre-mRNA is first spliced (C01), and the mature mRNA leaves the nucleus through the nuclear pores.
  • Bacteria have no nucleus, so their ribosomes start translating an mRNA while it is still being transcribed.
  • Translation starts when the small ribosomal subunit binds the mRNA at the start codon, a tRNA carrying methionine pairs with it, and the large subunit joins.
  • An anticodon is the triplet of a tRNA that pairs with a codon, complementary and antiparallel: codon 5'-AUG-3' pairs with anticodon 3'-UAC-5' (written 5'-CAU-3').
  • Elongation: the tRNA whose anticodon fits the next codon brings its amino acid, the rRNA joins it to the chain with a peptide bond, the ribosome moves three bases on, and the empty tRNA leaves to be reloaded.
  • Termination: no tRNA fits a stop codon; a release protein binds instead, the chain is released and the subunits come apart.

Translation (original diagram). The ribosome reads the mRNA 5'→3' in triplets (codons). Each tRNA pairs its anticodon with the complementary codon and delivers one amino acid; the rRNA of the large subunit links the amino acids with peptide bonds, so the chain grows by one amino acid per codon.

  • Several ribosomes read one mRNA at the same time (a polysome), so one mRNA produces many copies of the protein.
  • Proteins for use in the cytoplasm, such as the enzymes of glycolysis, are made on free ribosomes. Proteins for export, for the cell membrane or for lysosomes start with a signal sequence that docks their ribosome onto the rough endoplasmic reticulum (ruw endoplasmatisch reticulum, RER).
  • The chain is threaded into the RER, where it folds and gets disulfide bridges (zwavelbruggen, outcome 3) and often sugar groups; transport vesicles take it to the Golgi apparatus (golgi-systeem), which modifies, sorts and packs proteins into vesicles, and secretory vesicles release them by exocytosis (B02).
  • Example: a β-cell in the pancreatic islets makes insulin at the RER as one folded chain with disulfide bridges. In the Golgi apparatus and its vesicles a middle piece is cut out, leaving two chains of 21 and 30 amino acids (51 in total), which are released when blood glucose rises.
  • Cells that secrete a lot of protein, such as antibody-producing plasma cells, are packed with RER and have a large Golgi apparatus.
  • Genes on a plasmid are transcribed and translated in the same way, which is how bacteria with a recombinant plasmid produce a human protein such as insulin.
  • DNA polymerase doesn't take part in protein synthesis: it builds new DNA during replication (E01) and in PCR, extending a primer with DNA nucleotides.
  • Trap: don't confuse DNA polymerase with RNA polymerase. RNA polymerase transcribes a gene into RNA (with U), starting at a promoter without a primer; DNA polymerase copies DNA (with T) and needs a primer.

3. Primary structure determines shape and function

  • A protein has four levels of folding: primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure. The primary structure (primaire structuur) is the amino acid sequence, held together by peptide bonds (CCVX: “peptide binding”, peptidebinding). (CvTE M1.2 spec 3)
  • Every amino acid has an amino group (–NH₂), a carboxyl group (–COOH) and a side group (R) on one carbon atom. The 20 side groups differ: hydrophobic (valine, leucine), polar (serine), charged (glutamic acid −, lysine +) or with sulfur (cysteine, –SH). The Binas table of amino acids gives their structural formulas.
  • A peptide bond forms by condensation between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next, releasing water: glycine + alanine → glycylalanine + water, C₂H₅NO₂ + C₃H₇NO₂ → C₅H₁₀N₂O₃ + H₂O (chemistry C01).
  • Hydrolysis is the reverse: digestive enzymes break peptide bonds by adding water.
  • Secondary structure (secundaire structuur): the backbone folds locally into an α-helix (spiral) or a β-sheet (pleated sheet), held by hydrogen bonds between the C=O and N–H groups of the peptide bonds. Hair keratin is mostly α-helix, silk mostly β-sheet.
  • Tertiary structure (tertiaire structuur): the whole chain folds into a 3D shape, held by bonds between side groups (hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds between + and − groups, disulfide bridges), with the hydrophobic side groups clustered inside, away from water.
  • A disulfide bridge or sulfur bridge (zwavelbrug) is a covalent S–S bond formed by oxidation of the –SH groups of two cysteines. It is much stronger than the other bonds and staples parts of one chain, or two chains, together, as in hair keratin and antibodies.
  • Quaternary structure (quaternaire structuur): several polypeptide chains fit together into one protein; haemoglobin has four chains (two α, two β), each with a haem group that binds O₂.
  • The folded shape decides the function: an enzyme's active site, a receptor's binding site and a channel's pore only work in the right shape, and that shape follows from the sequence.
  • Example: in sickle-cell anaemia one base change turns codon 6 of β-globin from GAG (glutamic acid, charged) into GUG (valine, hydrophobic). At low O₂ the haemoglobin molecules stick together into fibres, and the red blood cells become sickle-shaped and block small vessels.
  • Denaturation (denaturatie): heat, extreme pH or heavy-metal ions break the weak bonds that hold the secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure, so the protein loses its shape and function, as when egg white sets on cooking or an enzyme stops working above its optimum temperature (B02).
  • Trap: denaturation doesn't break peptide bonds: the primary structure stays intact and only the folding is lost. Breaking peptide bonds is hydrolysis.

4. Proteins determine the structure and function of biological units

  • Proteins build cells and do most of their work, so the set of proteins a cell makes determines the structure and function of its organelles, and through them of tissues and organs. (CvTE M1.2 spec 4)
  • Enzymes speed up specific reactions because their active site fits one substrate: lactase splits lactose in the small intestine (B02, chemistry E02).
  • Structural proteins give shape and strength: collagen in tendons, bone and skin, keratin in hair and nails, and tubulin in the microtubules of the cytoskeleton.
  • Membrane proteins decide what enters and leaves a cell and which signals it notices: channels, carriers, pumps such as the Na/K pump (natrium/kalium-pomp), and receptors (D02).
  • Motor proteins move things: myosin pulls on actin filaments in muscle contraction, and kinesin carries vesicles along microtubules.
  • Other proteins transport substances (haemoglobin), act as hormones (insulin) or defend the body (antibodies, B05).
  • At organ level: dystrophin links the actin cytoskeleton inside a muscle fibre, through the cell membrane, to the extracellular matrix (tussencelstof) outside. Without it the membrane tears during contraction, the fibres die and the muscles weaken (Duchenne muscular dystrophy).
  • Different cell types (celtypen) make different proteins, which explains their different structures and functions (C01).
  • Trap: genes don't code for carbohydrates, fats or pigments directly; they code for the enzymes that make them. That's how a gene can change a non-protein trait, such as the type of starch in a potato (C01).

Specimen contexts

  • Duchenne muscular dystrophy (health): mutations in the dystrophin gene, often deletions of exons that shift the reading frame, cause an early stop codon and no dystrophin; the gene lies on the X chromosome, so the disease mostly affects boys. Experimental DNA therapies such as exon skipping make the splicing machinery skip an extra exon, which restores the reading frame and gives a shorter but partly working dystrophin, as in the milder Becker form. This uses B1.1 outcome 3 (finding the mutation) and B1.2 outcomes 1–4.
  • Bureau GGO and GM crops (food production): the assessment checks which DNA was inserted (with PCR and sequencing), which new protein the crop makes, whether that protein could be toxic or cause allergies, and whether the gene could spread to wild relatives. Bt maize, for example, makes a protein from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis that kills certain caterpillars. This uses B1.1 outcome 3, B1.2 outcomes 1–4 and D01.
  • Functional foods (food production): changing DNA changes which enzymes a crop makes, and so its composition; Golden rice has added genes for the enzymes that make β-carotene (provitamin A) in the grain. This uses B1.2 outcomes 1, 2 and 4 and D01.

CCVX versus the Dutch syllabus

  • In both: DNA and RNA structure, the functions of DNA, mRNA, tRNA and rRNA, nuclear, mitochondrial and chloroplast DNA, the ways to determine a base sequence (plasmid, primer, PCR, sequencing, restriction enzyme), the triplet code, transcription and translation with RER, Golgi apparatus, strands and reading direction, DNA polymerase, and the four levels of protein structure with peptide bonds.
  • Dutch syllabus only: the chemistry terms atom, molecule, ion, molecular formula, structural formula and hydrogen bond (waterstofbrug) in M1.1 specs 1–2, and the disulfide bridge (zwavelbrug) in M1.2 spec 3. The notes explain hydrogen bonds and disulfide bridges; the general chemistry is in chemistry B03 and chemistry G01.
  • CCVX only: nucleosomes (the CvTE has them in M4.1 spec 4), cDNA (CvTE M3.1 spec 2) and repetitive DNA (not in the CvTE syllabus at all); all three are explained above.

questions.questionHtml:
Biologists isolate DNA from a bacterium that lives in hot springs at about 75 °C. Analysis shows that 37% of its bases are cytosine.

Give the percentages of the other three bases in this DNA. Explain your answers.
questions.answerHtml: Guanine pairs with cytosine, so %G = %C = 37%. The remaining bases: 100 − (37 + 37) = 26%, so %A = %T = 13%.
questions.solutionHtml: Guanine pairs with cytosine, so %G = %C = 37%. The remaining bases: 100 − (37 + 37) = 26%, so %A = %T = 13%. Marking: • G = 37% with reference to base pairing (1) • A + T = 26% (1) • A = T = 13% (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Biologists isolate DNA from a bacterium that lives in hot springs at about 75 °C. Analysis shows that 37% of its bases are cytosine.

A second bacterial species, from pond water at 20 °C, has DNA of which 26% of the bases are cytosine. Explain which of the two DNA samples will separate into single strands at the lower temperature when heated.
questions.answerHtml: The pond-water DNA separates at the lower temperature.
questions.solutionHtml: The pond-water DNA separates at the lower temperature. It has fewer G–C pairs (52%) than the hot-spring DNA (74%); G–C pairs are held by three hydrogen bonds and A–T pairs by two, so DNA richer in G–C needs more heat (energy) to separate. Marking: • correct choice, pond-water DNA (1) • G–C has three hydrogen bonds, A–T two, so more energy is needed with more G–C (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Biologists isolate DNA from a bacterium that lives in hot springs at about 75 °C. Analysis shows that 37% of its bases are cytosine.

A fragment of the hot-spring DNA of exactly 1000 base pairs has the same base composition as the whole DNA of this bacterium. Calculate the total number of hydrogen bonds in this fragment.
questions.answerHtml: The fragment has 1000 base pairs = 2000 bases. Composition: 37% C and 37% G → 740 G–C pairs; 13% A and 13% T → 260 A–T pairs. Hydrogen bonds: 740 × 3 + 260 × 2 = 2220 + 520 = 2740.
questions.solutionHtml: The fragment has 1000 base pairs = 2000 bases. Composition: 37% C and 37% G → 740 G–C pairs; 13% A and 13% T → 260 A–T pairs. Hydrogen bonds: 740 × 3 + 260 × 2 = 2220 + 520 = 2740. Marking: • correct numbers of G–C and A–T pairs (740 and 260) (1) • correct calculation and answer 2740 (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Biologists isolate DNA from a bacterium that lives in hot springs at about 75 °C. Analysis shows that 37% of its bases are cytosine.

Does the rule "%A = %T and %G = %C" also hold for the mRNA of this bacterium? Explain.
questions.answerHtml: No. mRNA is single-stranded, so there is no complementary strand to enforce pairing; %A need not equal %U and %G need not equal %C.
questions.solutionHtml: No. mRNA is single-stranded, so there is no complementary strand to enforce pairing; %A need not equal %U and %G need not equal %C. Marking: • no, with reference to the single strand (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Since the 1980s, human insulin has been produced by bacteria such as E. coli. The bacteria are not given the human insulin gene as it occurs in the chromosome, but a cDNA copy of it, made from mRNA that was isolated from β-cells of the pancreatic islets.

Explain why the bacteria are given a cDNA copy made from mRNA instead of the gene as it occurs in the human chromosome.
questions.answerHtml: The chromosomal insulin gene contains introns, and E. coli cannot remove introns (no splicing). cDNA is copied from mature mRNA, so it contains only the exons and can be expressed correctly in bacteria.
questions.solutionHtml: The chromosomal insulin gene contains introns, and E. coli cannot remove introns (no splicing). cDNA is copied from mature mRNA, so it contains only the exons and can be expressed correctly in bacteria. Marking: • human gene contains introns / bacterial expression needs exons only (1) • cDNA is made from mature (spliced) mRNA (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Since the 1980s, human insulin has been produced by bacteria such as E. coli. The bacteria are not given the human insulin gene as it occurs in the chromosome, but a cDNA copy of it, made from mRNA that was isolated from β-cells of the pancreatic islets.

Name the enzyme that is used to make cDNA from mRNA, and name the group of viruses this enzyme originally comes from.
questions.answerHtml: Enzyme: reverse transcriptase. Origin: retroviruses.
questions.solutionHtml: Enzyme: reverse transcriptase. Origin: retroviruses. Marking: • reverse transcriptase (1) • retroviruses (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Since the 1980s, human insulin has been produced by bacteria such as E. coli. The bacteria are not given the human insulin gene as it occurs in the chromosome, but a cDNA copy of it, made from mRNA that was isolated from β-cells of the pancreatic islets.

The cDNA is built into a plasmid before it is brought into the bacteria. Give two properties that a plasmid must have to be usable for this.
questions.answerHtml: Any two of: an origin of replication, so the bacterium copies the plasmid; one or more restriction sites, to insert the cDNA; a marker gene, for example for antibiotic resistance, to select bacteria that took up the plasmid; a promoter that works in the host cell.
questions.solutionHtml: Any two of: an origin of replication, so the bacterium copies the plasmid; one or more restriction sites, to insert the cDNA; a marker gene, for example for antibiotic resistance, to select bacteria that took up the plasmid; a promoter that works in the host cell. Marking: • a first correct property (1) • a second, different correct property (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Since the 1980s, human insulin has been produced by bacteria such as E. coli. The bacteria are not given the human insulin gene as it occurs in the chromosome, but a cDNA copy of it, made from mRNA that was isolated from β-cells of the pancreatic islets.

The bacterial cells translate the human mRNA code into exactly the same amino-acid sequence as human cells do. Explain how that is possible.
questions.answerHtml: The genetic code is (almost) universal: each codon codes for the same amino acid in bacteria and in humans.
questions.solutionHtml: The genetic code is (almost) universal: each codon codes for the same amino acid in bacteria and in humans. Marking: • universal genetic code (1)

questions.questionHtml:
A forensic laboratory finds a tiny blood stain. For the DNA profile, one region of 400 base pairs is multiplied with the polymerase chain reaction (PCR). At the start there is exactly one double-stranded DNA molecule of the region, plus an excess of primers, free DNA nucleotides and Taq polymerase.

PCR repeats one cycle of three temperature steps. Name these three steps and describe what happens to the DNA or the primers in each step.
questions.answerHtml: Denaturation, about 95 °C: the strands separate (hydrogen bonds break). Annealing, about 50–65 °C: the primers pair with their complementary sequences on both strands. Extension, about 72 °C: Taq polymerase builds the new strands from the primers with free nucleotides.
questions.solutionHtml: Denaturation, about 95 °C: the strands separate (hydrogen bonds break). Annealing, about 50–65 °C: the primers pair with their complementary sequences on both strands. Extension, about 72 °C: Taq polymerase builds the new strands from the primers with free nucleotides. Marking: • denaturation with strand separation at high temperature (1) • annealing = primer binding at lowered temperature (1) • extension = synthesis by (Taq) polymerase (1)

questions.questionHtml:
A forensic laboratory finds a tiny blood stain. For the DNA profile, one region of 400 base pairs is multiplied with the polymerase chain reaction (PCR). At the start there is exactly one double-stranded DNA molecule of the region, plus an excess of primers, free DNA nucleotides and Taq polymerase.

Calculate the number of double-stranded copies of the 400-bp region that is present in theory after 25 cycles, at 100% efficiency. Give your answer in the form 4.2 × 10⁷ (one decimal × 10 to a power).
questions.answerHtml: Each cycle doubles the number of molecules: after 25 cycles, 2²⁵ = 33,554,432 ≈ 3.4 × 10⁷ copies.
questions.solutionHtml: Each cycle doubles the number of molecules: after 25 cycles, 2²⁵ = 33,554,432 ≈ 3.4 × 10⁷ copies. Marking: • use of 2²⁵ (1) • answer in correct form, 3.4 × 10⁷ (1)

questions.questionHtml:
A forensic laboratory finds a tiny blood stain. For the DNA profile, one region of 400 base pairs is multiplied with the polymerase chain reaction (PCR). At the start there is exactly one double-stranded DNA molecule of the region, plus an excess of primers, free DNA nucleotides and Taq polymerase.

Two different primers are needed for each PCR. Explain why one primer is not enough, and explain why the polymerase can only extend a primer at its 3' end.
questions.answerHtml: The two strands are antiparallel, and the target is copied on both strands in opposite directions, so each strand needs its own primer at the other end of the target.
questions.solutionHtml: The two strands are antiparallel, and the target is copied on both strands in opposite directions, so each strand needs its own primer at the other end of the target. DNA polymerase builds a new strand only 5' → 3' and needs a free 3'-OH end to attach the next nucleotide, so it extends the primer's 3' end. Marking: • two strands copied in opposite directions / both ends of the target must be defined (1) • synthesis only 5'→3' (1) • extension from a free 3' end (1)

questions.questionHtml:
A forensic laboratory finds a tiny blood stain. For the DNA profile, one region of 400 base pairs is multiplied with the polymerase chain reaction (PCR). At the start there is exactly one double-stranded DNA molecule of the region, plus an excess of primers, free DNA nucleotides and Taq polymerase.

A PCR primer is about 20 nucleotides long. Show with a calculation that a random sequence of 20 bases is expected to occur at most once by chance in the human genome of 3.2 × 10⁹ base pairs.
questions.answerHtml: With 4 possible bases per position there are 4²⁰ ≈ 1.1 × 10¹² different sequences of 20 bases.
questions.solutionHtml: With 4 possible bases per position there are 4²⁰ ≈ 1.1 × 10¹² different sequences of 20 bases. The genome offers only ~3.2 × 10⁹ starting positions; chance of a given 20-mer occurring once is ≈ 3.2 × 10⁹ / 1.1 × 10¹² ≈ 3 × 10⁻³, far below 1. Marking: • 4²⁰ ≈ 1.1 × 10¹² (1) • comparison with 3.2 × 10⁹ and conclusion (1)

questions.questionHtml:
To check a genetically modified plant, biologists map the DNA around an inserted gene. A linear DNA fragment from the plant has a total length of 10.0 kilobase pairs (kb). The fragment contains two sites for the restriction enzyme HindIII, at 2.5 kb and at 7.5 kb from the left end, and one site for the restriction enzyme EcoRI at 4.0 kb from the left end.

The fragment is cut with HindIII only. Give the number of fragments and the length of each.
questions.answerHtml: Three fragments: 2.5 kb, 5.0 kb and 2.5 kb.
questions.solutionHtml: Three fragments: 2.5 kb, 5.0 kb and 2.5 kb. Marking: • three fragments (1) • lengths 2.5 – 5.0 – 2.5 kb (1)

questions.questionHtml:
To check a genetically modified plant, biologists map the DNA around an inserted gene. A linear DNA fragment from the plant has a total length of 10.0 kilobase pairs (kb). The fragment contains two sites for the restriction enzyme HindIII, at 2.5 kb and at 7.5 kb from the left end, and one site for the restriction enzyme EcoRI at 4.0 kb from the left end.

The fragment is cut with HindIII and EcoRI together. Give the number of fragments and the length of each.
questions.solutionHtml: Four fragments: 2.5 kb (0–2.5), 1.5 kb (2.5–4.0), 3.5 kb (4.0–7.5) and 2.5 kb (7.5–10.0). Marking: • four fragments (1) • lengths 2.5 – 1.5 – 3.5 – 2.5 kb (1)

questions.questionHtml:
To check a genetically modified plant, biologists map the DNA around an inserted gene. A linear DNA fragment from the plant has a total length of 10.0 kilobase pairs (kb). The fragment contains two sites for the restriction enzyme HindIII, at 2.5 kb and at 7.5 kb from the left end, and one site for the restriction enzyme EcoRI at 4.0 kb from the left end.

EcoRI cuts between the G and the A of the sequence 5'-GAATTC-3' on both strands, so it leaves short single-stranded overhangs. Explain what these "sticky ends" are and why they are useful when a DNA fragment is built into a plasmid.
questions.answerHtml: A sticky end is the short single-stranded overhang left after the staggered cut (here AATT).
questions.solutionHtml: A sticky end is the short single-stranded overhang left after the staggered cut (here AATT). Two molecules cut with the same enzyme have complementary overhangs that base-pair, so the fragment fits into the plasmid in a fixed position and DNA ligase can seal the backbones. Marking: • single-stranded overhang from the staggered cut (1) • complementary pairing and sealing by ligase (1)

questions.questionHtml:
To check a genetically modified plant, biologists map the DNA around an inserted gene. A linear DNA fragment from the plant has a total length of 10.0 kilobase pairs (kb). The fragment contains two sites for the restriction enzyme HindIII, at 2.5 kb and at 7.5 kb from the left end, and one site for the restriction enzyme EcoRI at 4.0 kb from the left end.

After cutting, the fragments are separated with gel electrophoresis. Explain why DNA fragments move towards the positive pole and why shorter fragments move faster through the gel than longer fragments.
questions.answerHtml: The phosphate groups give DNA a negative charge, so fragments migrate to the positive pole in the electric field.
questions.solutionHtml: The phosphate groups give DNA a negative charge, so fragments migrate to the positive pole in the electric field. The gel acts as a sieve: shorter fragments pass through the pores more easily and therefore move faster (travel further in the same time). Marking: • negative charge (phosphate) and movement to the positive pole (1) • sieving effect: shorter fragments move faster (1)

questions.questionHtml:
A research group studies a small human gene. Part of the template (matrix) strand of this gene reads:

3'-TAC AGC TTA ATC-5'

Give the sequence of the mRNA that is transcribed from this template strand, written with the 5' and 3' ends.
questions.answerHtml: 5'-AUG UCG AAU UAG-3'.
questions.solutionHtml: 5'-AUG UCG AAU UAG-3'. (Template A→U, T→A, C→G, G→C; the mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template strand.) Marking: • all four triplets correct in the right order (1) • correct 5' and 3' ends (1)

questions.questionHtml:
A research group studies a small human gene. Part of the template (matrix) strand of this gene reads:

3'-TAC AGC TTA ATC-5'

Give the sequence of the coding strand of this part of the gene, written with the 5' and 3' ends.
questions.answerHtml: 5'-ATG TCG AAT TAG-3' (same as the mRNA, with T instead of U).
questions.solutionHtml: 5'-ATG TCG AAT TAG-3' (same as the mRNA, with T instead of U). Marking: • sequence correct with T (1)

questions.questionHtml:
A research group studies a small human gene. Part of the template (matrix) strand of this gene reads:

3'-TAC AGC TTA ATC-5'

Name the DNA sequence to which RNA polymerase binds to start transcription of a gene.
questions.answerHtml: The promoter.
questions.solutionHtml: The promoter. Marking: • promoter (1)

questions.questionHtml:
A research group studies a small human gene. Part of the template (matrix) strand of this gene reads:

3'-TAC AGC TTA ATC-5'

In eukaryotic cells, transcription takes place in the nucleus and translation on ribosomes in the cytoplasm. Explain how the mRNA gets from the nucleus to the ribosomes, and name one advantage of this arrangement for the cell.
questions.answerHtml: The mRNA leaves the nucleus through the nuclear pores into the cytoplasm, where ribosomes are.
questions.solutionHtml: The mRNA leaves the nucleus through the nuclear pores into the cytoplasm, where ribosomes are. Advantage (any one): the mRNA can first be spliced/processed and quality-checked; the DNA itself stays protected in the nucleus; the cell can regulate which mRNAs are exported or broken down. Marking: • through nuclear pores (1) • a correct advantage, e.g. processing/quality control or protection of DNA (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Fish in polar seas produce small antifreeze proteins. Part of the mRNA for one of these proteins reads:

5'-AUG UGU GGU CCA AAG UAA-3'

Genetic code (from the BINAS table): AUG Met, UGU Cys, GGU Gly, CCA Pro, AAG Lys, AGG Arg, UAA stop.

Give the amino-acid sequence that is translated from this mRNA.
questions.answerHtml: Met–Cys–Gly–Pro–Lys (translation stops at UAA).
questions.solutionHtml: Met–Cys–Gly–Pro–Lys (translation stops at UAA). Marking: • all five amino acids correct (1) • in the correct order, with translation stopped at UAA (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Fish in polar seas produce small antifreeze proteins. Part of the mRNA for one of these proteins reads:

5'-AUG UGU GGU CCA AAG UAA-3'

Genetic code (from the BINAS table): AUG Met, UGU Cys, GGU Gly, CCA Pro, AAG Lys, AGG Arg, UAA stop.

Give the anticodon of the tRNA that delivers lysine, written with the 3' and 5' ends, and explain what this anticodon does during translation.
questions.answerHtml: Anticodon 3'-UUC-5'. The anticodon pairs complementarily (and antiparallel) with the codon AAG in the mRNA, so the tRNA delivers its amino acid (lysine) at exactly the right position.
questions.solutionHtml: Anticodon 3'-UUC-5'. The anticodon pairs complementarily (and antiparallel) with the codon AAG in the mRNA, so the tRNA delivers its amino acid (lysine) at exactly the right position. Marking: • anticodon 3'-UUC-5' (1) • complementary pairing with the codon places the amino acid correctly (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Fish in polar seas produce small antifreeze proteins. Part of the mRNA for one of these proteins reads:

5'-AUG UGU GGU CCA AAG UAA-3'

Genetic code (from the BINAS table): AUG Met, UGU Cys, GGU Gly, CCA Pro, AAG Lys, AGG Arg, UAA stop.

Explain why translation stops at the codon UAA and not at another codon.
questions.answerHtml: UAA is a stop codon: no tRNA has the matching anticodon, so no amino acid is delivered; instead a release factor binds and the finished chain is released.
questions.solutionHtml: UAA is a stop codon: no tRNA has the matching anticodon, so no amino acid is delivered; instead a release factor binds and the finished chain is released. Other codons each have a matching tRNA. Marking: • no tRNA fits a stop codon (1) • release factor / chain released (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Fish in polar seas produce small antifreeze proteins. Part of the mRNA for one of these proteins reads:

5'-AUG UGU GGU CCA AAG UAA-3'

Genetic code (from the BINAS table): AUG Met, UGU Cys, GGU Gly, CCA Pro, AAG Lys, AGG Arg, UAA stop.

A mutation changes the codon AAG into AGG. Give the consequence for the amino-acid sequence, and give the name of this type of point mutation.
questions.answerHtml: AAG (Lys) becomes AGG (Arg): one amino acid is replaced by another; this is a missense mutation (a substitution).
questions.solutionHtml: AAG (Lys) becomes AGG (Arg): one amino acid is replaced by another; this is a missense mutation (a substitution). Marking: • Lys replaced by Arg (1) • missense/substitution (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Researchers study mutations in a human gene for an enzyme involved in pigment formation. Part of the coding strand of the healthy allele reads:

5'-ATG GGC TTT CAG TAA-3'

Genetic code (from the BINAS table): AUG Met, GGC Gly, GGT Gly, UUU Phe, UUG Leu, CAG Gln, UAG stop, UAA stop.

In one patient, the sixth base of this fragment, C, is replaced by T, so the second codon reads GGT instead of GGC. Give the consequence for the amino-acid sequence and explain your answer using the table.
questions.answerHtml: No consequence: GGC and GGT both code for glycine, so the amino-acid sequence is unchanged (silent mutation).
questions.solutionHtml: No consequence: GGC and GGT both code for glycine, so the amino-acid sequence is unchanged (silent mutation). The genetic code is degenerate. Marking: • no change in the sequence (1) • both codons code for Gly / code is degenerate (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Researchers study mutations in a human gene for an enzyme involved in pigment formation. Part of the coding strand of the healthy allele reads:

5'-ATG GGC TTT CAG TAA-3'

Genetic code (from the BINAS table): AUG Met, GGC Gly, GGT Gly, UUU Phe, UUG Leu, CAG Gln, UAG stop, UAA stop.

In a second patient, the codon CAG has become TAG. Give the consequence for the length of the protein chain and explain why.
questions.answerHtml: The protein becomes shorter by at least one amino acid (the chain ends after Met–Gly–Phe).
questions.solutionHtml: The protein becomes shorter by at least one amino acid (the chain ends after Met–Gly–Phe). Coding TAG gives mRNA UAG, a stop codon, so translation stops at the fourth codon instead of after Gln. Marking: • new stop codon UAG (1) • premature end of translation, shorter chain (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Researchers study mutations in a human gene for an enzyme involved in pigment formation. Part of the coding strand of the healthy allele reads:

5'-ATG GGC TTT CAG TAA-3'

Genetic code (from the BINAS table): AUG Met, GGC Gly, GGT Gly, UUU Phe, UUG Leu, CAG Gln, UAG stop, UAA stop.

In a third patient, a single nucleotide in the second codon has been deleted. Explain why this mutation usually has much more serious consequences for the protein than the substitution in item bio-b01-q25, and explain why a deletion of exactly three nucleotides in this region is usually less serious than a deletion of one.
questions.answerHtml: Deleting one nucleotide shifts the reading frame for the whole rest of the mRNA: every downstream codon is read differently, so most or all following amino acids are wrong and a stop codon usually appears early. Deleting exactly three nucleotides removes one complete codon: the frame is kept and only one amino acid is missing.
questions.solutionHtml: Deleting one nucleotide shifts the reading frame for the whole rest of the mRNA: every downstream codon is read differently, so most or all following amino acids are wrong and a stop codon usually appears early. Deleting exactly three nucleotides removes one complete codon: the frame is kept and only one amino acid is missing. Marking: • frameshift changes all downstream codons (1) • many wrong amino acids / often early stop codon (1) • 3-nucleotide deletion removes one codon but keeps the frame (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Lysozyme is an enzyme in tears and saliva that breaks down bacterial cell walls. It is a single polypeptide chain of 130 amino acids with four disulfide bridges.

Name the four levels of protein structure, and for each level name the bond(s) that maintain it.
questions.answerHtml: Primary structure: the amino-acid sequence, held by peptide bonds.
questions.solutionHtml: Primary structure: the amino-acid sequence, held by peptide bonds. Secondary structure: α-helix/β-sheet of the backbone, held by hydrogen bonds. Tertiary structure: overall folding of one chain, held by bonds between side groups (hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bridges, hydrophobic interactions). Quaternary structure: several chains together, held by bonds between the chains (non-covalent bonds and sometimes disulfide bridges). Marking: • primary with peptide bonds (1) • secondary with hydrogen bonds (1) • tertiary with side-group bonds (1) • quaternary with several chains (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Lysozyme is an enzyme in tears and saliva that breaks down bacterial cell walls. It is a single polypeptide chain of 130 amino acids with four disulfide bridges.

A student claims: "When lysozyme is boiled, its peptide bonds break and the protein falls apart into loose amino acids." Assess this claim.
questions.answerHtml: The claim is wrong.
questions.solutionHtml: The claim is wrong. Boiling breaks the weak bonds (such as hydrogen bonds) of the secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure: the protein denatures and loses its shape, but the peptide bonds of the primary structure stay intact; they are covalent and are broken only by hydrolysis. Marking: • claim rejected (1) • denaturation concerns folding, peptide bonds need hydrolysis (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Lysozyme is an enzyme in tears and saliva that breaks down bacterial cell walls. It is a single polypeptide chain of 130 amino acids with four disulfide bridges.

Antibodies consist of four polypeptide chains that stay together in the bloodstream for weeks. Explain which level of protein structure is involved here, and explain the role of disulfide bridges.
questions.answerHtml: Quaternary structure (four polypeptide chains).
questions.solutionHtml: Quaternary structure (four polypeptide chains). Disulfide bridges are covalent S–S bonds between cysteines of chains; they are much stronger than hydrogen bonds or hydrophobic interactions, so the four chains stay firmly connected. Marking: • quaternary (1) • disulfide bridges are covalent and strong, holding the chains together (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Lysozyme is an enzyme in tears and saliva that breaks down bacterial cell walls. It is a single polypeptide chain of 130 amino acids with four disulfide bridges.

In sickle-cell anaemia, the sixth amino acid of the β-chain of haemoglobin, glutamic acid, is replaced by valine. Glutamic acid has a charged side group; valine has a hydrophobic side group. Explain how this single substitution can make haemoglobin molecules stick together into fibres when the oxygen concentration is low.
questions.answerHtml: Valine is hydrophobic where glutamic acid was charged.
questions.solutionHtml: Valine is hydrophobic where glutamic acid was charged. The hydrophobic valine sits on the outside of the chain and sticks to hydrophobic parts of neighbouring haemoglobin molecules; at low oxygen concentration the molecules aggregate into fibres (and the red blood cells deform). Marking: • valine is hydrophobic, glutamic acid charged (1) • hydrophobic attraction to neighbouring molecules (1) • aggregation into fibres at low O₂ (1)

questions.questionHtml:
In Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), a deletion in the dystrophin gene shifts the reading frame of the mRNA downstream of the deletion, so that a stop codon appears far too early and no working dystrophin is made. In the milder Becker form, the deletion leaves the reading frame intact and a shorter but partly functional dystrophin is produced. Medicines called antisense oligonucleotides (AONs) are short synthetic RNA-like molecules. They bind to one chosen exon in the pre-mRNA, so that the splicing machinery skips that exon as well.

In this simplified example, a patient has a deletion of exons 49 and 50; after splicing, exon 48 is joined to exon 51 in a shifted reading frame.

Explain what is meant by "shifted reading frame" and why such a shift usually leads to an early stop codon.
questions.answerHtml: The reading frame is the grouping of the mRNA into triplets (codons), fixed by the start codon.
questions.solutionHtml: The reading frame is the grouping of the mRNA into triplets (codons), fixed by the start codon. After a shift, three bases are grouped differently, so all downstream codons change. Three of the 64 codons are stop codons, so in a shifted frame a stop codon appears by chance within about 21 codons on average, far sooner than the real end of the gene. Marking: • frame = grouping into triplets (1) • downstream codons all read differently (1) • high chance of an early stop codon (1)

questions.questionHtml:
In Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), a deletion in the dystrophin gene shifts the reading frame of the mRNA downstream of the deletion, so that a stop codon appears far too early and no working dystrophin is made. In the milder Becker form, the deletion leaves the reading frame intact and a shorter but partly functional dystrophin is produced. Medicines called antisense oligonucleotides (AONs) are short synthetic RNA-like molecules. They bind to one chosen exon in the pre-mRNA, so that the splicing machinery skips that exon as well.

In this simplified example, a patient has a deletion of exons 49 and 50; after splicing, exon 48 is joined to exon 51 in a shifted reading frame.

The patient is treated with an AON against exon 51. Explain how this treatment can restore the reading frame downstream of exon 48.
questions.answerHtml: The AON binds exon 51 in the pre-mRNA and hides it from the splicing machinery, so exon 51 is skipped too.
questions.solutionHtml: The AON binds exon 51 in the pre-mRNA and hides it from the splicing machinery, so exon 51 is skipped too. Splicing then joins exon 48 directly to exon 52 (in this example), which restores the original grouping into codons downstream of the junction. Marking: • exon 51 is skipped through binding of the AON (1) • exon 48 joined to exon 52 (1) • original reading frame restored downstream (1)

questions.questionHtml:
In Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), a deletion in the dystrophin gene shifts the reading frame of the mRNA downstream of the deletion, so that a stop codon appears far too early and no working dystrophin is made. In the milder Becker form, the deletion leaves the reading frame intact and a shorter but partly functional dystrophin is produced. Medicines called antisense oligonucleotides (AONs) are short synthetic RNA-like molecules. They bind to one chosen exon in the pre-mRNA, so that the splicing machinery skips that exon as well.

In this simplified example, a patient has a deletion of exons 49 and 50; after splicing, exon 48 is joined to exon 51 in a shifted reading frame.

Explain why the treated patient still does not produce completely normal dystrophin, and why the effect can nevertheless resemble the milder Becker form.
questions.answerHtml: The protein still lacks the amino acids that were encoded by exons 49–51, so it is not completely normal.
questions.solutionHtml: The protein still lacks the amino acids that were encoded by exons 49–51, so it is not completely normal. But the reading frame is intact and the rest of the protein is normal, so it is a shortened, partly functional protein — comparable to a Becker-type dystrophin, which also has an internal deletion with an intact frame. Marking: • amino acids of the deleted exons are missing → shorter protein (1) • intact frame gives a partly functional protein, like Becker (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Maize with a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt maize) produces a protein, Bt toxin, that kills certain caterpillars. A Dutch assessment bureau evaluates an application to grow Bt maize.

The Bt gene comes from a bacterium but is correctly translated in the cells of the maize plant. Explain how that is possible.
questions.answerHtml: The genetic code is (almost) universal: every codon means the same amino acid in the bacterium and in maize, so plant ribosomes translate the bacterial gene into the same protein.
questions.solutionHtml: The genetic code is (almost) universal: every codon means the same amino acid in the bacterium and in maize, so plant ribosomes translate the bacterial gene into the same protein. Marking: • universal code (1) • plant translation uses the same codon–amino-acid pairs (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Maize with a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt maize) produces a protein, Bt toxin, that kills certain caterpillars. A Dutch assessment bureau evaluates an application to grow Bt maize.

Describe the steps needed to construct a plasmid that makes maize cells produce Bt toxin, from isolating the Bt gene to the production of the protein in the plant cell. Name the enzymes involved and explain why the Bt gene alone is not enough: a second DNA element must be placed in front of it.
questions.answerHtml: Steps: cut the Bt gene out of the bacterial DNA with a restriction enzyme; open a plasmid with the same restriction enzyme; join gene and plasmid with DNA ligase (sticky ends pair); place a promoter in front of the gene that is active in plant cells, because the bacterial promoter is not (or badly) recognised by plant RNA polymerase; multiply the plasmid in bacteria and/or transfer it into plant cells, where the gene is transcribed (RNA polymerase) and translated on ribosomes.
questions.solutionHtml: Steps: cut the Bt gene out of the bacterial DNA with a restriction enzyme; open a plasmid with the same restriction enzyme; join gene and plasmid with DNA ligase (sticky ends pair); place a promoter in front of the gene that is active in plant cells, because the bacterial promoter is not (or badly) recognised by plant RNA polymerase; multiply the plasmid in bacteria and/or transfer it into plant cells, where the gene is transcribed (RNA polymerase) and translated on ribosomes. Marking: • restriction enzyme for cutting gene and plasmid (1) • ligase for joining (1) • promoter active in plant cells must be added (1) • gene then transcribed and translated in the plant (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Maize with a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt maize) produces a protein, Bt toxin, that kills certain caterpillars. A Dutch assessment bureau evaluates an application to grow Bt maize.

The bureau wants to know the exact base sequence at the site where the new DNA is inserted in the maize DNA. Name the technique that determines this sequence, and name the technique used first to multiply the small amount of DNA at that site.
questions.answerHtml: Determination of the sequence: (DNA) sequencing.
questions.solutionHtml: Determination of the sequence: (DNA) sequencing. Multiplying the small amount first: PCR. Marking: • sequencing (1) • PCR (1)

questions.questionHtml:
Maize with a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt maize) produces a protein, Bt toxin, that kills certain caterpillars. A Dutch assessment bureau evaluates an application to grow Bt maize.

Bt toxin is eaten by humans in maize products. Explain what normally happens to proteins such as Bt toxin during digestion, and explain why the bureau nevertheless compares the amino-acid sequence of Bt toxin with the sequences of known allergens.
questions.answerHtml: Dietary proteins are normally hydrolysed into single amino acids and short peptides by proteases in the stomach and small intestine, so an intact active protein is not taken up.
questions.solutionHtml: Dietary proteins are normally hydrolysed into single amino acids and short peptides by proteases in the stomach and small intestine, so an intact active protein is not taken up. But some proteins resist digestion, and resistant fragments can trigger allergy; a sequence resembling a known allergen is a warning sign, so the comparison is a precaution. Marking: • hydrolysis by digestive (protease) enzymes (1) • intact protein normally not absorbed (1) • some proteins resist digestion, hence the allergen comparison (1)
